# Synthetic dyes and coal-tar chemistry (`synthetic_dyes`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: needs nitric_acid, sulphuric_acid, distillation; helped by gas_lighting, coke_iron, organic_structure_theory, mordant_dyeing
- Core idea: The black tar left over from making coke and coal gas is a store of ring compounds. Distilling it gives benzene; nitric with sulphuric acid turns that into nitrobenzene, and iron filings with acid reduce this to aniline. Oxidising impure aniline gave Perkin a purple that dyes silk fast, and systematic variation then produced every colour, including the natural dyes alizarin and indigo. The same chemistry and the same firms later gave drugs (aspirin, Salvarsan, the sulphonamides), photographic chemicals and explosives.
- Pitfalls:
  - Telling it as luck alone; the lesson is that research on a waste product pays, once structure theory guides it.
  - Benzene, aniline and several dye intermediates are poisons; dye workers later suffered bladder cancer.
  - Nitration runs away if not cooled; nitro compounds can explode.
  - Overlooking the composition of commercial aniline: related compounds in Perkin’s starting material contributed to the mauveine mixture.
- History: europe: 1834 Runge finds aniline and phenol in coal tar; 1856 Perkin's mauve (London); 1859 magenta; 1868–1869 Graebe and Liebermann synthesise alizarin; 1880 Baeyer synthesises indigo, sold by BASF from 1897; 1909 Ehrlich's Salvarsan; india: after 1897 – synthetic indigo destroys the Bengal and Bihar indigo plantations within two decades
- Read:
  - Simon Garfield, Mauve: How One Man Invented a Colour That Changed the World (2000)
  - Anthony S. Travis, The Rainbow Makers: The Origins of the Synthetic Dyestuffs Industry in Western Europe (1993)
